title: AI self-evolution could close the loop in as little as six months, but models will quietly drift off course
dek: The inflection point for RSI is a model that can handle long-horizon tasks. Apodex's chief scientist says the self-evolution loop could close in as little as six months, but recursive drift and model taste still need humans minding them for a long time to come.
why: A frontline researcher breaks down the RSI technical path, verification methods and timeline. High information density, and direct material for understanding the real progress of model self-evolution.
who: AI founders, large-model researchers, investors, and engineers following agent architectures.
skip: The roughly 5-minute comparison of the two founders' styles at the end can be skipped; it has little to do with the main thread.

points.h: Recursive self-improvement became possible because of long-horizon tasks
points.body: Self-evolution is not a new idea. Two or three years ago there were already approaches like LM-as-optimizer and agent optimizer, but back then a model could only optimize for two or three hours; one small mistake would compound on itself and it could not keep iterating. What is different this year is that models have gotten stronger and can complete long-horizon tasks that take a human 1.5 hours or even 12 hours, so they can self-correct many times within a single task, and the "R" in recursive finally holds up. At Anthropic, 80% of code is written by Claude — it is precisely coding ability that makes it natural for a model to train itself.

points.h: Three technical bottlenecks stand in the way of long-horizon tasks
points.body: Long-horizon tasks are not just a context-length problem. First, standard attention has quadratic complexity, so million-token inference is extremely resource-hungry and needs architectural innovation. Second, long-context support alone is not enough: the model must have been trained on very long data, otherwise it goes out-of-distribution. Third, the training and inference infra also has to change, including GPU optimization and kernel-level code. Stack those three difficulties together and the difficulty of long-horizon tasks rises exponentially. Simon adds that even with a million-token context, truly ultra-long-horizon tasks still need agent architecture and memory mechanisms to digest.

points.h: Recursive drift is the fundamental obstacle to self-evolution
points.body: When a model generates its own training data, reasoning errors accumulate and amplify across generations — that is recursive drift. Apodex's countermeasure is verification: code and math are easy to verify, using test scripts or formal proofs, so they are relatively controllable; but the tests themselves can be too broad or too narrow, and subtle drift still occurs. So Apodex specifically trains verification ability, and during reinforcement learning it has the judge learn alongside, to keep the model from learning bad behaviors like reward hacking.

points.h: Verification relies on sub-agents checking each other plus redundancy
points.body: The name Apodex comes from the Greek word for "proof." Verification methods differ by domain: code uses unit tests, math uses formal proofs, but more problems depend on human judgment. Apodex 1.0 uses an agent team: first decompose the problem, one sub-agent solves it and another sub-agent verifies it separately, avoiding context contamination; then have multiple agents work the same problem to produce redundancy, with a global agent judging which answer is more accurate. During training it also has agents judge the credibility of information sources — a forum, for instance, is less reliable than a textbook.

points.h: The three self-evolution paths have very different moats
points.body: Beibing divides self-evolution into three paths: pretraining, post-training, and harness (scaffolding). Evolving at the harness level is the cheapest — you can do it just by calling APIs — and the open-source community and academia have produced plenty of results there, so the moat is the shallowest. Post-training is the more core and more difficult battlefield: you first have to diagnose model defects, create targeted problems, and verify training results, which takes a lot of resources. Pretraining is currently mostly toy-level tasks and has not really scaled to product level. Apodex does all three; post-training and scaffolding are like the left foot stepping on the right foot, iterating alternately. To judge a company's capability, first ask which layer it evolves at.

points.h: Why an agent team beats a single smart AI
points.body: Simon states it plainly: one smart AI cannot beat a team that checks each other. The reason is the nature of self-attention — the longer the context, the worse attention works, and linear attention does not solve ultra-long context either, so a single model has a ceiling under current technology, just as a person's working memory is limited and needs notes. So multiple agents must divide the work and share information through memory mechanisms to handle ultra-long-horizon problems. Model capability and agent engineering are one plus one greater than two; agent teams in vertical domains still have a moat, though the scaffolding has to be fine-tuned as models iterate every month.

points.h: The hard part of a discovery model is verification, not generation
points.body: Generative models already have mature training recipes, but a discovery model's goal is not to generate answers but to propose and verify out-of-distribution hypotheses. The first step requires a creative hypothesis, and the hard part is that it is far from the pretraining data; the second step is judging whether the hypothesis holds, which brings us back to verification. You can use deep research to gather existing information to assist the hypothesis, and you can write code to run simulations to build confidence. But unknown domains often have no standard answer and no trustworthy simulation environment, so self-evolution is Apodex's main route toward a Heavy Duty Solver.

points.h: A six-month loop, but drift will take years
points.body: Beibing expects the first self-evolution loop to close in as little as six months to a year: in some domain (coding, say) the model finds its own problems, generates its own training data, verifies itself, and iterates one round. But the recursive part of RSI requires many rounds, and recursive drift is still unsolved; he is confident it can be fully solved within a few years. What keeps him up at night is not knowing whether the model has drifted off course while self-evolving — both safety goals and performance goals can drift. For now the only option is to manually read model outputs every day and intervene in agent behavior; in the future, "distilling yourself" could inject that monitoring ability into the model and speed up the process.

terms.def: The ability of a model to train itself and improve in a loop.
When a model self-generates training data, errors accumulate across generations and it gradually deviates from the goal.
Apodex's goal — a general model that solves hard problems for which humans have no standard answer.
A model that does not rely on known answers but proposes and verifies new hypotheses.
A collaborative system in which multiple sub-agents divide work and verify each other, used for ultra-long tasks and verification.
